pages.text:
*Days without rain: 114. Buckets from the spring: 14.*

On the morning of the hundred-and-fourteenth dry day, Mei woke to the sound of nothing. It was a very particular nothing. It was the sound of a roof that expected rain and was, once again, disappointed.

Her grandmother was already up, cutting a notch in the bamboo stick that hung by the kitchen door. Nainai (which is what you call your father's mother) cut one notch every morning, and the stick was now so covered in them it looked like a tiny fence. Nainai was small and straight-backed, with grey hair pinned in a bun and a dark blue jacket with cloth knots for buttons, and she cut each notch the way other people close a door: firmly, without slamming.

"Hundred and fourteen," she said.

"I know," said Mei, who had been counting too.

Mei was eleven, small for it, with two short black braids tied with red string and a nose that had gone brown from a whole spring of squinting at an empty sky. Her name meant plum blossom, the flower that opens in the snow when nothing else dares. She had never thought it fit her very well.
pages.image: Inside a simple farmhouse kitchen, small straight-backed Nainai cuts a notch in a bamboo stick hanging by the kitchen door while Mei, seen from the side in her faded blue padded jacket, watches her in the pale morning light, just the two of them in the room.

pages.text:
Tao clumped in next, in his yellow rain boots. Tao was seven, round-faced and gap-toothed, and he had worn those boots every single day since the drought began.

"For luck," he said, before anyone asked. Nobody had asked for a hundred and fourteen days.

"They are making the floor wet," said Nainai, which was a joke, because the floor had not been wet since New Year, and Tao laughed so hard he had to sit down on the step.

Breakfast was noodles, and not ordinary ones. Nainai had pulled them so thin they hung from the chopsticks like white hair. Dragon's-whisker noodles, she called them, and she always made them at this time of year, because in six days it would be the second day of the second month, when the old people say the dragon raises his head. That was when he was supposed to wake from his long winter sleep, and the rain was supposed to follow.

"Some dragon," said Tao, slurping.

Nainai looked at the pale window. "Slurp quietly," she said. "He may be listening."
pages.image: At a small wooden table in a farmhouse kitchen, Mei in her faded blue padded jacket, Tao, a round-faced gap-toothed seven-year-old boy in a green tiger T-shirt and bright yellow rubber rain boots, and Nainai with a grey bun and a dark blue jacket eat thin white noodles from blue-and-white bowls in soft morning light, Tao slurping with a grin.

pages.text:
After breakfast Mei took her small bamboo pole across her shoulders, a bucket hanging from each end, and walked to the spring. Every household in Bamboo Ridge Village did the same, twice a day, and the path had been worn smooth by feet and pails and patience.

It followed the stream, or what used to be the stream. Now it was a wide road of grey stones, dry as bones, with a few white dragonfly wings pressed into the mud like pages in a book. Tao trotted alongside it, counting frogs.

"Zero," he reported. "Zero. Zero. Oh! No. A stick."

The spring was tucked beside the little stone Dragon King shrine, where the mountain still let out a thin, thoughtful trickle of water. A line of neighbors waited there, each with a pole and a pair of buckets, and nobody was talking much. They were being polite in the special way people are polite when they are worried: passing the ladle, saying "after you", and not looking at how little was in the rock pool.

Mei took her place at the end of the line. A bucket, she had learned, filled slowly when you were watching it.
pages.image: A line of villagers with bamboo shoulder poles and wooden buckets waits quietly beside a tiny stone shrine where a thin trickle of water runs into a rock pool, a dry stream bed of grey stones beside the path, Mei in a faded blue padded jacket and straw hat with a small pole at the end of the line and Tao in yellow rain boots beside her, steep green mountains behind in soft morning mist.

pages.text:
From the spring you could see all of Bamboo Ridge climbing the hill in steps: the terraces, the tile roofs, the tea bushes in their neat green rows. Up the slope, in the seedling beds where the rice was supposed to be growing tall and bright, the plants had gone the colour of old straw. Even the tea leaves curled up at the edges, brittle as paper.

Uncle Shi, the village head, was standing at the top bed with his battered steel thermos. He was a round, tired man in a grey jacket and a blue cap, and he worried on behalf of the whole village, which is an enormous job for one person. As Mei watched, he unscrewed the lid of his thermos, looked at the little yellow seedlings, and very carefully poured a thin stream of his own tea on them.

Then he seemed to realize what he was doing. He stood there with the empty thermos, and even from far away Mei could see the embarrassment go right through him.

She thought it was the saddest present she had ever seen anyone give.
pages.image: On steep green rice terraces above a tile-roofed village, round tired Uncle Shi in a grey jacket and a blue cap pours tea from a battered steel thermos onto a bed of yellowing rice seedlings, brittle curled tea bushes in rows around him, Mei seen small in the distance below with her bamboo pole, misty mountains behind.

pages.text:
They got home with fourteen buckets between them for the day, which was exactly enough and not one drop more. Mei set down her pole and pressed her thumb into the middle of her palm, the way she did when something sat too heavily on her chest. She did not know she did it. Everyone else did.

"Is the dragon even real?" asked Tao, pulling off one boot to check whether it was still yellow inside. It was.

Mei opened her mouth to say she did not know, and the words went somewhere she could not follow. She shut it again.

Nainai was wringing out a cloth over the smallest bucket, catching every drop. "Water finds a way," she said, without looking up. "Sometimes it needs help finding the way."

She said it lightly, the way you say something you have said many times, and hoped it was true. Mei looked out of the window at the wide, pale blue sky over the mountain, and searched all of it, from one side to the other, for a single cloud.

There was not one.
pages.image: Inside the farmhouse kitchen, Nainai with a grey bun and dark blue jacket wrings a cloth into a small wooden bucket while Mei in a faded blue padded jacket stands by the window with her thumb pressed into her palm looking out at a huge cloudless pale blue sky over green mountains, Tao sitting on the step holding a yellow rain boot.
